# **1\.  Introduction**

## **1.1  Overview**

*Introduce the project in 150–200 words. What is the system, what problem does its AI solve, and who is it for? Assume the reader has not seen your proposal.*

| “Guess Who I Am” is an Akinator-style game in which the player secretly thinks of a well-known Pakistani personality or place, and the computer works out who or what it is by asking yes/no questions. After every answer, the program updates how likely each candidate is and then picks the question that will narrow the field the most. It is meant for anyone curious about Pakistani people, history, and geography, and no prior knowledge is needed to play. A plain program could only follow a fixed script of questions, which fails as soon as the player answers “probably” or gives a mistaken answer. The AI instead reasons under uncertainty, keeps a probability for every candidate and chooses a new best question on every turn. |
| :---- |

# **2\.  Problem Formulation**

## **2.1  Problem Statement**

*Describe the problem in 120–180 words. Why is it hard — the size of the search space, the uncertainty, the number of interacting constraints? Give a concrete example of an instance your system solves.*

| Identifying a hidden person or place from yes/no answers sounds easy, but the space of possible interrogations is enormous. With a knowledge base of 40 attributes (for example, “is alive”, “is a politician”, “is in Punjab”), the number of ordered ways to choose 20 of them is 40\!/20\!, about 3 × 10^29, so trying every sequence is hopeless. The information is also uncertain: players answer “probably”, misremember facts, or disagree with our data, so a single wrong answer can derail a rigid decision tree. The questions interact too, because a good question depends on every answer already given and on which candidates are still likely. Today, people playing such games simply guess at random or ask questions in a fixed order, which wastes turns and breaks on noisy answers. Solving this is worthwhile because it shows how probability and information theory let a program get the most out of every answer, while making Pakistani culture and geography more interactive to explore. |
| :---- |

## **2.3  Problem Representation**

*For a data-driven project, use the state row for the input features and the goal row for the target being predicted.*

| Element | Representation in your code |
| :---- | :---- |
| **State representation** | A probability distribution over all N candidates, plus the questions asked so far and the answers received. |
| **Actions / moves** | Ask one unused attribute question, or make a final guess. |
| **Initial state** | Uniform prior over all candidates (each 1/N) with no questions asked. |
| **Goal or terminal test** | Top candidate’s probability reaches 0.85, and the player confirms the guess, or 20 questions have been asked. |
| **Cost, utility, fitness or evaluation** | Each question costs 1\. Candidate questions are scored by expected information gain, i.e. the expected drop in entropy of the distribution. |

# **3\.  System Design and Architecture**

## **3.1  Overall Architecture**

*Explain in 100–150 words how the parts of your system fit together — environment, agents, algorithms, experiment runner and visualisation — and how data flows through them, from input to stored results. Then place your architecture or data-flow diagram below.*

| The system follows a modular architecture in which the KnowledgeBase acts as the central data source. Initially, build\_knowledge\_base.py generates a CSV dataset containing 161 records and 47 attributes. The KnowledgeBase module loads this dataset and provides information to the other components. The BeliefState maintains the probabilities and predictive information about possible answers, while the QuestionSelector selects the next question using Information Gain or Random selection. The SimulatedPlayer provides answers, and the GameAgent manages the questioning process and generates guesses. The Streamlit UI allows the human player to interact with the agent through five answer buttons. Finally, the Evaluator compares the agent's guesses with the simulated player's answers and generates CSV results and four charts for performance analysis.  |

## **4.2  Technique Details**

*Fill one block for each AI technique you implemented, including the one you compared against. Copy the block if you have more than two.*

| Technique 1 |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| Name | Bayesian Reasoning with Information Gain  |
| Own code or library | Implemented from scratch in Python. Uses the project's belief-state calculations and entropy formula; no external AI or machine-learning library is used for question selection.  |
| Heuristic, evaluation, fitness or model | Entropy is used to measure uncertainty in the candidate probability distribution. Information Gain is calculated as the difference between current entropy and expected entropy after a question. The question with the highest expected Information Gain is selected.  |
| Key parameters and values used | Five answer options (Yes, Probably, Don't know, Probably not, No); initial uniform prior; maximum 20 questions; confidence threshold of 0.85; 40 attributes (according to the dataset description).  |
| Time and space cost | For $C$ candidates, $Q$ available questions and $A$ possible answers, selection requires approximately $O(QCA)$ time when expected posterior entropy is evaluated across candidates and answers. Additional working space is approximately $O(C+Q)$, excluding the stored knowledge base and belief distribution. |

| Technique 2 |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| Name | Random Question Selection  |
| Own code or library | Implemented from scratch using Python's random module. |
| Heuristic, evaluation, fitness, or model | No heuristic is used. The strategy randomly selects one of the available unanswered questions. It serves as the baseline for evaluating Information Gain.  |
| Key parameters and values used | Same candidate knowledge base, five answer options, maximum 20 questions and confidence threshold of 0.85. Random seed of 42 was used in experiments for reproducibility.  |
| Time and space cost | Approximately $O(Q)$ time to identify available unanswered questions, followed by $O(1)$ random selection. Additional space is approximately $O(Q)$ for the available question list.  |

## **4.3  Key Implementation Details**

*Choose the most interesting part of your implementation — usually the heart of your core algorithm — and explain how it works and why you built it that way. Include a short code excerpt of ten to fifteen lines at most; do not paste whole files.*

 def update(self, attribute: str \| int, answer: str \| int) \-\> None:  
        """Apply Bayes' rule in place and remember the question and answer."""  
        self.probs \= self.posterior(attribute, answer)  
        self.asked.append(self.kb.attribute\_index(attribute))  
        self.answers.append(ANSWERS\[\_answer\_index(answer)\])

   
   
 

| The code updates the probability of every candidate based on the answer received from the user. It first retrieves the candidate's previous probability, also called the prior, and calculates the likelihood of receiving the user's answer if that candidate were correct. The prior is multiplied by the likelihood to obtain an unnormalized updated probability. After processing all candidates, the values are normalized by dividing each by their total sum. This ensures that the probabilities form a valid distribution and add up to 1\. The question and answer are also recorded so that the system does not repeat previously asked questions and can maintain its answer history. This approach was chosen because users may provide uncertain or incorrect answers, so candidates should not be immediately eliminated. Instead, their probabilities are adjusted according to the evidence received, allowing the system to maintain uncertainty throughout the game. |
| :---- |

## **6.4  Discussion**

*In 120–180 words: which approach performed best and why, in terms of the problem formulated in Chapter 2? What was the trade-off between solution quality and speed? Did anything surprise you, and is the difference between approaches large enough to be more than chance?*

| Information Gain performed better than Random Selection for the candidate-guessing problem because it selects questions that are expected to reduce uncertainty and help identify the correct candidate more efficiently. It achieved a success rate of 66.46%, compared to 21.74% for Random Selection. It also required fewer questions on average (16.59 compared to 20). However, this improvement came with a speed trade-off. Information Gain took approximately 0.136 seconds per game, while Random Selection took only 0.002 seconds because it does not perform entropy calculations. One thing that stood out was the large difference in success rates, showing the benefit of choosing questions strategically rather than randomly. Although Information Gain clearly performed better in these results, we cannot confidently conclude that the difference is statistically significant without further repeated experiments and statistical testing. Overall, Information Gain is more suitable for this project because achieving accurate guesses with fewer questions is more important than having the fastest question-selection process.  |
| :---- |

## **7.3  Limitations and Ethical Considerations**

*In 100–150 words: where does your AI fail or become too slow, and why? Whose data does the system use and with what consent? Could its decisions be unfair or biased, and against whom? What is the consequence of a wrong prediction or a poor decision, and what would you tell a user about its limitations?*

| Our AI system has some limitations. Its accuracy depends on the quality and completeness of the knowledge base, which currently contains 161 Pakistani personalities and places with 47 attributes. It may fail to identify candidates with missing or incorrect information, especially when several candidates have similar attributes. The system can also become less accurate when users provide incorrect or uncertain answers. Its performance is limited to a maximum of 20 questions. The system uses a manually created dataset and does not collect personal user information or require sensitive data. Although Bayesian reasoning reduces uncertainty, incorrect predictions are still possible. Bias may occur because the knowledge base focuses mainly on Pakistani personalities and locations. We inform users that predictions are estimates and that the final guess may not always be correct.  |

## **8.1  Challenges Faced**

*The two genuine difficulties you met and how you solved them — for example a search that was too slow until you added pruning, or a heuristic that turned out not to be admissible. Honest difficulty, well explained, reads far better than a claim that everything went smoothly.*

| One challenge was integrating the different components of the game, particularly the question-selection strategies, belief state, and game agent. Each component had to use the same question and answer representations for the game to work correctly. This was resolved by testing the components individually and then integrating them through the game agent. Another challenge was handling incorrect guesses and updating the knowledge base without losing the information collected during gameplay. The user's previous answers needed to be mapped to the corresponding candidate attributes, and new candidates had to be saved without creating duplicates. This was addressed by using the recorded questions and answers to construct a new candidate and updating the CSV knowledge base.  |
| :---- |

## **8.2  Conclusion and Future Work**

*In 100–150 words, state what was achieved against the objectives in Section 1.2, then name two or three concrete improvements you would make with more time.*

| The project successfully developed an interactive guessing game that identifies Pakistani personalities and places using Bayesian reasoning. A knowledge base was created, and the system updates candidate probabilities based on user responses. Two question-selection strategies, Information Gain and Random Selection, were implemented and compared through simulated experiments. A Streamlit interface was also developed to allow users to play the game, view predictions, and add incorrectly guessed candidates to the knowledge base. The project demonstrated that Information Gain generally performs better than random question selection in reducing uncertainty and identifying candidates. However, the system is limited by the accuracy and coverage of its knowledge base. In future, we would expand and verify the dataset, improve question selection using more informative attributes, and conduct larger experiments with real users to evaluate the system's performance under realistic conditions.  |
| :---- |
